findings.question: q-earth-science-astronomy-stars-and-galaxies-0001
findings.problem: This makes fusion universal to stars. A white dwarf, explicitly included in the lesson, shines by releasing stored heat rather than ongoing fusion. The note reinforces a false absolute while correcting the temperature misconception.
findings.fix: Replace with: Many stars shine by fusion, but their surface temperatures can differ. Check the color-temperature order.

findings.question: q-earth-science-astronomy-stars-and-galaxies-0008
findings.quote: The $2.5$ million light-years is the distance to the nearby Andromeda galaxy, not the width of the Milky Way.
findings.problem: This discusses the number used in the wrong choices and explains why those choices are wrong. The requested explanation must explain only the correct answer.
findings.fix: Keep only the sentence identifying the Milky Way as a spiral galaxy about 100,000 light-years across.

findings.question: q-earth-science-astronomy-stars-and-galaxies-0009
findings.quote: This gives dark matter a way to shine. Many dark objects can be seen by reflected light. Check that dark matter does not give off light.
findings.problem: The proposed check does not rule out the choice about reflected light. An object can reflect light without producing its own light; the Moon is a familiar example. The note needs to distinguish reflection from emission.
findings.fix: Explain that dark matter does not detectably reflect light either, and tell the student to check for evidence from its gravitational pull.

findings.question: q-earth-science-astronomy-stars-and-galaxies-0011
findings.quote: Check that a supernova belongs to a much more massive star.
findings.problem: This categorically assigns supernovae to much more massive stars. A Type Ia supernova instead involves a white dwarf in a binary system. The question concerns the ordinary evolution of a Sun-like star, so the note should limit its claim to that path.
findings.fix: Say: Check that a Sun-like star normally sheds its outer layers as a planetary nebula and leaves a white dwarf.

findings.question: q-earth-science-astronomy-stars-and-galaxies-0014
findings.quote: Its stars are at very different distances from Earth.
findings.problem: This turns a possibility into an absolute. Two stars in the same constellation can be a physical binary and lie at essentially the same distance from Earth. The keyed choice correctly says they can be at very different distances.
findings.fix: Say: Stars in the same constellation can be at very different distances. Appearing close in the sky does not tell us their distances.
